summary: A 1975 description of Network UNIX, a version of UNIX used as a mini-host on the ARPANET. It covers its standard input and output, Telnet, NCP, hardware and software needs, reliability and availability.

eli5.summary: This note describes how a UNIX computer was made to join the early network, and what it could and could not do.

questions: unix on the arpanet mini host
subtitle: A version of UNIX that treats network connections as special files, integrating ARPANET protocols into the filesystem

tldr.problem: UNIX was designed for a single computer with local peripherals. Connecting it to the ARPANET required network protocols, but integrating them in a way that fit the UNIX philosophy of uniform interfaces was non-trivial.
tldr.mechanism: Network UNIX treats network connections as special files in the filesystem. Just as /dev/mt0 represents a tape drive, /dev/net/harv represents a connection to Harvard. Programs use standard UNIX I/O calls (OPEN, READ, WRITE, CLOSE) to communicate over the network, with protocols like Telnet implemented as user programs.
tldr.outcome: Network protocols are integrated cleanly into UNIX, requiring only about 3.5K words of kernel code for the NCP kernel portion and 8.5K for the swappable NCP daemon. This elegant design proved influential on later operating systems.

today: Network UNIX pioneered the idea of treating network connections as uniform file-like objects, influencing the design of later systems. Today, similar concepts appear in UNIX sockets, BSD sockets, and the general principle of "everything is a file." The design proved that network protocols could be elegantly integrated into an operating system without sacrificing the OS's core philosophy.

sections.title: The Design Problem
sections.content:
RFC 681 describes how the UNIX time-sharing system was modified to work as a mini-host on the ARPANET. UNIX is a general-purpose operating system with strong principles around unified interfaces: reading from a file, from a terminal, from a network should all use the same basic mechanism. The challenge was integrating ARPANET protocols (IMP-to-Host, Host-to-Host, Telnet, and others) in a way consistent with UNIX philosophy.

UNIX treats everything as a file, accessed through four basic I/O calls: OPEN (connect), READ (receive data), WRITE (send data), and CLOSE (disconnect). The elegance would be lost if network I/O required a completely different interface.
sections.eli5: UNIX is very organized: everything is treated the same way. When the network had to be added, the designers wanted to keep that sameness.

sections.title: Network as Special Files
sections.content:
The solution is elegant: network connections are represented as special files in the filesystem. Just as the UNIX filesystem includes special files like /dev/mt0 (tape drive 0) and /dev/lp (line printer), Network UNIX adds special files under /dev/net/ for each remote host. For example, /dev/net/harv represents a connection to the PDP-10 at Harvard.

A user or program establishes a network connection simply by opening the appropriate special file:

filedes = OPEN("/dev/net/harv", 2)

If this returns a valid file descriptor (not minus one), the connection succeeded. If it returns minus one, the host is unreachable. Once open, reading from and writing to the file descriptor performs network I/O using the appropriate ARPANET protocols, just as reading from a disk file performs disk I/O.
sections.eli5: A connection to Harvard looks like a file named `/dev/net/harv`. You open it, read from it, write to it, and close it—just like a real file.

sections.title: Telnet and NCP Implementation
sections.content:
With network connections accessible as files, protocols like Telnet can be implemented as user programs instead of being built into the kernel. The Telnet program lets a user login to a remote UNIX system normally, then runs telnet to open a network connection. While connected, the user can still run local UNIX commands, with Telnet executing them in parallel using the UNIX shell mechanism.

The Network Control Program (NCP) is split into two parts to minimize kernel size (a critical concern on computers with limited memory). A 3.5K word kernel portion handles basic network operations and message switching. A separate 8.5K word daemon process (swappable, like any other user program) handles connection management and status traffic. The two communicate through a special file, keeping network functionality modular and memory-efficient.

The hardware used for development was a PDP-11/50 with 32K words of core memory, expandable to 48K, with multiple disk drives for user files, system files, and swap space. UNIX required the DEC memory management option to run at all.
sections.eli5: Telnet is just a regular program that uses these special network files. The kernel part is small, and the big part runs like a normal program, so it doesn't hog the kernel.

sections.title: Reliability and Future Plans
sections.content:
At the time of writing, Network UNIX had been running full-time for about four weeks, with three to four crashes per day (though many were hardware-related). After hardware reconfiguration, the crash rate dropped to about one per day with 2-3 minutes of downtime.

The team's future plans included extensive bandwidth and load testing, and expansion of the OPEN system call to support more parameterization: connections to specific sockets, simplex connections on existing socket pairs, and the ability to listen on local sockets. Beyond Telnet, the team planned to implement network mail, FTP and RJE as user programs.

Network UNIX software was developed without ARPA support but offered gratis to the ARPA community. Users had to license the base UNIX system from Bell Laboratories (nominal fee for universities, $20,000 for other institutions). The Center for Advanced Computation at the University of Illinois was willing to assist others in acquiring and installing the system.
sections.eli5: The system worked but crashed once a day. They planned to test more and add more features. They were willing to help other people set it up.
